newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Scotia eyed for pipeline progress.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Scotia eyed for pipeline progress.

text.p: Drug development group Scotia Holdings Plc will be watched closely for news of progress on its burgeoning drug pipeline when it reports interim results on Tuesday, analysts said on Friday.

Analysts are reluctant to give forecasts for half-year pretax losses, expected to widen to around 8.0 million pounds from 5.4 million a year earlier, as Scotia pushes its unconventional portfolio of drugs, based on fatty acids, to the market place.
They said the key figure of interest will be the rate at which Scotia is spending cash, which is estimated to be between 18 and 23 million pounds a year.
Yamaichi International analyst Erling Refsum said the group should have sufficient funding to get through the next two to three years without fresh cash injections.
Scotia has six drugs close to market, and a further 16 compounds all in earlier stages of development. It is planning a research and development update to coincide with results.
Stewart Adkins, analyst at Lehman Brothers, said he expects Scotia "to make a presentation on which products they can market themselves and which they will license out."

UBS analyst Mark Clark is hoping for signs that Scotia remains confident of winning regulatory approval for its diabetic drug, EF4, this year as well of progress on finding a new partern for the project.

Analysts are also looking for progress on EF13, currently being tested for pancreatic cancer. Some say the drug could be a rival to British Biotech Plc's potential blockbuster cancer product, Marimastat.

There are also hopes it will say more about anti-eczema prodict Epogam, which is already approved. Sales have been limited, partly because effective treatment requires 12 capusules a day, making it unsuitable for children. A new liquid formation could transform its prospects.
Lehman's Adkins said he hopes to hear that Scotia has applied for European approval of its EF27 drug, which alleviates the side-effects of radiotherapy, particularly skin damage.
